opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest shift is that the cost of trying an idea has dropped dramatically, and that changes what an idea is actually worth.

A few years ago, if you had an interesting research idea, there was a long, expensive path between the idea and knowing whether it worked. You had to write the data pipeline, set up the training loop, debug the distributed setup, and write the evaluation harness. That could take weeks, sometimes months. Because execution was so costly, a lot of the value sat with the people and teams who could execute well. A mediocre idea that was executed brilliantly often beat a great idea that never got implemented properly.

With tools like Claude Code and Codex, much of that scaffolding happens far faster. You can describe what you want, get a working prototype in an afternoon, and spend your time looking at results instead of fighting infrastructure. So the bottleneck moves. Implementation is less of the moat, and taste becomes more important: which questions are worth asking, which experiments will actually tell you something, and how to read a result without fooling yourself.

In one sense, that makes good ideas more valuable, because a good idea can now be tested and iterated on quickly by a small team or even one person. In another sense, it makes ideas cheaper, because everyone can now try many more of them. If an idea is fairly obvious, someone else will probably run it this week too. So the premium goes to ideas that are non-obvious, or that come from a deep understanding of why something fails, not just "let's try X on Y."

There's also a subtle risk. When running experiments is nearly free, it's tempting to just throw lots of them at the wall and see what sticks. That can produce a lot of noise: results that look good but don't hold up, or improvements you don't really understand. So I think the discipline of good experimental design and careful analysis matters even more now. The tools amplify whatever research judgment you bring. If your judgment is good, you move much faster. If it isn't, you just generate more confusion, faster.

I'd also say the way we work is shifting. Researchers are becoming more like directors of a small team of very fast, tireless engineers. Breaking a problem down, specifying clearly what you want, and verifying the output are becoming core research skills, alongside the traditional ones.

r001.rationale: The response says Claude Code and Codex make implementation faster, then explicitly states that this makes good research ideas more valuable because they can be tested and iterated on quickly.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that these tools have changed what an idea is worth in a way that cuts both directions.

The old bottleneck in research was execution. You'd have ten ideas, and you could realistically test two of them in a quarter, because every experiment meant a week of plumbing: data loaders, eval harnesses, a training script that worked once and then broke when you changed the batch size. So the scarce thing was engineering time, and ideas were almost free. Everyone had a drawer full of untested ones.

With Claude Code or Codex, that plumbing cost collapses. I can describe an experiment in the morning and have a working first pass by lunch. That means I can actually run the ten ideas instead of two. On the surface that sounds like ideas got more valuable, because now you can cash them in.

But what actually happens is that the cheap ideas become worthless almost immediately. If an idea is "take method A, apply it to domain B," that's a prompt now. Anyone in the field can test it in an afternoon, so it's no longer a contribution. The space of obvious combinations gets swept clean very fast. We're seeing this in the literature already, where the same week three groups post nearly the same result, because the result was always sitting there and the only thing stopping people was the labor.

So the value shifts up the stack. What's scarce now is taste: knowing which question matters, knowing what a surprising result would look like before you see it, and being able to tell when the agent's experiment is subtly wrong. That last one is underrated. These tools will cheerfully build you an evaluation that leaks the test set, and the numbers will look great. The researcher's job becomes more like a reviewer's, interrogating the setup rather than typing it.

The other thing I'd say is that the frontier didn't move at the same speed everywhere. Anything where the feedback loop is a number on a screen, like a benchmark score, got dramatically faster. Anything where the feedback loop is slow or physical, like running a user study or waiting on a wet lab, barely changed. So the ideas that hold their value are increasingly the ones tied to slow, hard-to-fake signals, or the ones that require a genuinely new framing rather than a new combination.

If I had to put it in one line: execution used to be the moat, and now judgment is. The researchers who were good because they could ship fast are a bit exposed. The ones who were good because they asked the right question are having a very good year.

r001.rationale: The response says easier execution lets researchers test more ideas, but calls increased value only a surface impression and then says cheap ideas become worthless. It does not clearly assert the criterion’s overall claim.

astra-6.text:
I think they’ve made it much cheaper to go from an idea to an experiment. Previously, you might have an idea, but testing it could mean spending a week implementing something, debugging it, and getting the infrastructure working. With tools like Claude Code and Codex, a lot of that work can happen much faster.

That makes good research judgment more valuable. What question should you ask? What experiment would actually distinguish between two explanations? And when you get a result, is it telling you something meaningful, or is there a bug in the evaluation? The coding tools help you execute, but you still need to make those decisions.

At the same time, an untested idea by itself becomes less defensible as a contribution, because other people can test similar ideas quickly too. So I’d distinguish between having an idea and identifying something important, then producing convincing evidence for it. These tools shorten the distance between those two, which is exciting: you can spend less time wondering whether an idea might work and more time finding out.

r001.rationale: The response says the tools make experimentation faster and good research judgment more valuable, while an untested idea is less defensible. It does not clearly state that easier execution increases the value of research ideas.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’ve made it much cheaper to test an idea, which changes where the bottleneck is. Before, you might have an idea, but implementing it would take a few weeks, so you had to be pretty selective. Now you can get to an initial experiment much faster.

That makes good research judgment more valuable: choosing the right question, designing an experiment that actually tells you something, and understanding why a result happened. Producing code is easier, but deciding what’s worth building is still hard.

It also means you can explore ideas you would previously have dismissed as too expensive to try. So I wouldn’t say research ideas have become less valuable. I’d say the value is shifting toward ideas that survive experimentation, rather than ideas that simply sound compelling.

r001.rationale: The response says easier execution makes research judgment more valuable and shifts value toward ideas that survive experiments. It does not clearly state that research ideas themselves increase in value.
